newsitem.title: Bulgaria: Bulgarian parties meet president to discuss crisis.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian parties meet president to discuss crisis.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists and opposition parties gathered on Tuesday with President Petar Stoyanov to seek ways to defuse a month-long political crisis.
The meeting took place hours before a deadline for the Socialists to present a new government and against a backdrop of concern that violence will erupt should they try to cling to power.
Hundreds of anti-government protesters gathered outside the presidency building and chanted anti-communist slogans, keeping up 30 days of demonstrations to demand immediate elections.
Nikolai Dobrev, designated to form a new cabinet and serve as prime minister, met Stoyanov earlier but did not present his new cabinet as expected.
Instead they discussed the crisis. Stoyanov then called a meeting of his advisory National Security Council, including all parliamentary group leaders as well as the army and police.

The Socialists, the ex-communists, have until midnight to present a cabinet or return the mandate which Stoyanov gave them last week. If they give up the mandate, it would most likely mean a quick general election.
Officials said Stoyanov and Dobrev would again raise the possibility at the meeting of forming an all-party coalition to pass emergency economic reforms and then hold elections.
But main opposition leader Ivan Kostov said on entering the meeting that he expected the Socialists to give up the mandate and accept elections almost two years ahead of schedule.
The Socialists have been reeling from a heavy presidential election defeat in November, followed a month later by the resignation of prime minister Zhan Videnov.

The Socialists are blamed for the devastated economy, with the month-on-month rate of inflation at 50 percent and the lev currency in freefall. The deepening crisis since Videnov resigned has dealt the economy further blows.
The European Union and the International Monetary Fund have said they cannot help until Bulgaria has a stable government.

Protesters kept up strikes and blockades around Bulgaria, some staying out all night in sub-zero temperatures. But some protesters dismantled barricades on Tuesday after warnings that police might move in to clear them.
Student organisers said they would lift roadblocks, except at Eagles' Bridge and in front of the university, this evening to ease access to Sofia for protesters from provincial towns.
If the Socialists present a cabinet, it will face a vote of confidence in parliament on Wednesday and protesters have vowed to stream into the capital and set up barricades around the building.

Athough some barricades came down, thousands of opposition supports swarmed central Sofia and tension was high as the country waited to see the outcome of the showdown between the Socialists and the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF).
The Socialists are deeply divided between hardliners who insist on forming a new cabinet and those who want to return the mandate.

They drafted a new cabinet on Monday, mostly old faces, and it must be presented by midnight on Tuesday at the latest. The decision to push ahead with a new government heightened tension throughout the country.
Dobrev and Socialist party leader Georgi Parvanov had to slip into both meetings with Stoyanov through sidedoors on Tuesday to avoid raucous protesters outside the main entrance.
Kostov told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday that tension had risen noticeably and the protests could easily get out of control.
"We have appealed to police and protesters to avoid any violence because we are all part of the suffering Bulgarian nation," he said.
Public transport did not run in Sofia for a second day.
Protesters from Doupnitsa, where townspeople have blocked road and rail routes to Greece for a week, said they were heading for Sofia to set up barricades outside parliament.
